text: The last two chapters built identity verification — who's asking, from what device, under what risk. This chapter turns to how much that identity actually gets once it's verified, starting with the network itself. Course nine already taught you real segmentation: hub-spoke VNets, NSGs, Transit Gateway route tables. What this lesson adds is the gap that segmentation alone leaves open, and why the fix has a name of its own: micro-segmentation.

Picture a properly segmented network: a web tier, an app tier, a data tier, each with its own NSG. That NSG does real work at the boundary between tiers — a compromised web server genuinely cannot reach the data tier directly. But look inside the app tier itself. It might hold forty different services, all sitting under one shared NSG rule that lets the whole subnet talk to itself. The tier boundary held. Nothing inside that tier was protected from anything else inside it.

Micro-segmentation closes exactly that gap by shrinking the unit policy is written against. Instead of a rule covering an entire subnet, a micro-segmented policy names one workload: the payments-api service can reach the orders-db service on port 5432, specifically, and nothing else in that subnet gets the same permission. The blast radius from one compromised service shrinks from the whole tier down to the small handful of workloads it was ever explicitly allowed to call.

That only works if policy can survive workloads moving — and in any autoscaled or containerized environment, they move constantly, picking up new IP addresses as they get rescheduled. An IP-based rule can't keep up with that. So micro-segmentation attaches policy to a workload identity instead: a certificate, or a signed label like app=payments-api, env=prod. The policy travels with the workload wherever it lands, because it's attached to what the workload is, not to its current address.

This is the same tenet Chapter 1 introduced for user access, now applied to traffic between workloads instead of traffic from a person: every request gets evaluated and strictly enforced, nothing inside the environment is implicitly trusted just because it's already inside. Next lesson takes that same move and applies it to how users themselves reach private applications — replacing a traditional VPN with a software-defined perimeter that doesn't expose the app to anyone it hasn't already authorized.
